blocks.title: Radiant flux intensity
blocks.text: Radiant flux intensity, F, is the amount of electromagnetic energy per unit area per unit time from a star that reaches the Earth's surface (or any point at a distance d from the star). It is a small fraction of the total luminosity.

For a star at a distance d, the radiant flux intensity is F = L / (4 pi d^2) (21.2), where L is the luminosity. As the luminosity of a star is constant, the radiant flux intensity follows an inverse-square law with distance (Fig 21.1): when the distance from the star is doubled (from r to 2r), the intensity falls to one-quarter; at three times the distance it falls by a factor of nine, and so on.

blocks.title: What 4 pi d^2 is
blocks.text: The book says that in F = L/(4 pi r^2), '4 pi r^2 is the surface area of the star'. Here the denominator is the area of an imaginary sphere of radius d (the distance from the star to the observer), over which the star's power has spread; it is not the star's own surface area.

blocks.alt: A star at the left sends light into a widening cone. At distances r, 2r and 3r the same beam passes through areas drawn as squares divided into 1, 4 and 9 small squares, labelled F, F/4 and F/9. Below: F = L/(4 pi d^2); standard candles (Cepheid variables, Type Ia supernovae) have known luminosity, so measuring F gives d = sqrt(L/4 pi F).
blocks.caption: The inverse-square law and standard candles (original diagram after Figs 21.1 and 21.2).
blocks.long_description: The same power spreads over an area that grows as the square of the distance, so each square metre receives less. Knowing how much power a standard candle emits, the measured flux tells us how far away it is.

blocks.text: The luminosity of a star is 4.50 x 10^26 W. It is 1.40 x 10^11 m from a planet. Calculate the radiant flux intensity at the planet's surface. Solution: F = L / (4 pi r^2) = 4.50 x 10^26 W / (4 x 3.14 x (1.40 x 10^11 m)^2) = 1.83 x 10^3 W m^-2.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: If Earth were twice as far from the Sun, the sunlight reaching it would be only one-quarter as intense; such low energy might have made the evolution of life impossible.

blocks.prompt: Two stars appear equally bright in the night sky, but one is 10 times farther away than the other. Which is more luminous, and by how much?
blocks.explanation: The farther star: for equal F, L is proportional to d^2, so it is 10^2 = 100 times more luminous.

items: F = L / (4 pi d^2): power per unit area at distance d.
Inverse-square law: double the distance, quarter the flux.
